headline: Bunker in the Breachways, Bass Gone Nocturnal, Fluke Chewing the Neap
subhead: The bait's stacking up in every breachway from Sakonnet to Napatree, and the bass have figured out the dark is safer than the daylight.
body_markdown:
Stood on the rocks at Napatree before first light Tuesday and watched a pod of peanut bunker come pouring out of the mouth of the breachway like someone pulled a plug. Thousands of them, balled up tight, nervous, with something underneath pushing them around. That something turned out to be a pack of schoolie-to-mid-thirties bass working the edge of the current seam where the outgoing water meets the open Sound. Same story at Watch Hill Point, same story down at the Weekapaug cut. The bait's here. The question this week has been figuring out when the fish are willing to eat it in daylight, because mostly, they aren't.

Water's been sitting warm along this whole stretch, low-to-mid 70s depending on where you check it, and that's pushed the keeper-class stripers into a strict low-light program. I'm not seeing much worth chasing between 9am and 6pm unless you're fishing deep structure, but dusk through dawn has been good and steady. My best window this week was the last hour of the outgoing into the start of the flood at Sakonnet Point — fished a black/purple 1.5-ounce bucktail with a white pork rind trailer off the rocks below the lighthouse, and picked off four bass in the 26-32 inch range in about ninety minutes, all on a slow bottom bump through the rip. Second Beach in Middletown has been giving up similar fish to guys soaking bunker chunks on fish-finder rigs off the sand right at the mouth of the Sakonnet River, fishing the last two hours of dark.

The moon just went first-quarter, so we're sliding into neap tides through the weekend — less current push, softer rips, which is actually working in our favor right now. Anything that depends on a hard-running rip to hold bait tight, like Beavertail or the Jamestown side of the East Passage, has widened out. The current's not screaming through there like it does on the new and full, so the bite window at those spots is longer and more forgiving. If you're throwing eels or swimbaits at night off Beavertail, you've got more time to work the water instead of one tight slack-into-flood window.

Fluke have been the one bite you can set your watch to, and daylight-friendly to boot. We said a week or two back that summer fluke fishing would keep building through August as the back-bay fish push out toward the inlets and ocean structure, and that's exactly what's playing out. The mid-bay drifts off Jamestown — the flats south of the Newport Bridge in 18 to 25 feet — have been holding solid numbers on the last of the outgoing and first hour of the incoming. White and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom, drifting with the current instead of fighting it. Mixed bag of shorts but enough keepers in the 18-20 inch range to make it worth staying with. Charlestown Breachway is doing the same thing on a smaller scale — work the deeper channel edge right where it dumps into the salt pond side, moving water only, dead water is dead water there.

Bluefish have shown up in patches, not everywhere, but where the bunker schools are thick — Second Beach, the stretch off Sachuest Point, and the beach in front of Weekapaug — you'll get slashing surface action for twenty, thirty minutes at a time before they push off. That matches what we've been seeing up and down the coast this month, bunker pods dragging blues along with them, and I expect that pattern to keep showing up here as long as the bait stays put and we don't get a blow that scatters it. Topwater poppers or a simple diamond jig with no tube, worked fast through the froth, is all you need when it happens. Just be ready — it's not a sit-and-wait bite, it's a run-and-gun one.

Tog are off the table right now — season's closed here till the first of August — but I've been out checking a few of my ledges anyway, just scouting. The rock piles off Newport's Ocean Drive and the drop just outside Watch Hill Cove are still holding bait and structure exactly like they should be, so when the season flips back on I've got a short list ready.

Too early yet for albies — that first push into the breachways is a September story around here, and I'm not seeing any scout fish or bait signs that say otherwise. But the water's warming the way it needs to, and by mid-to-late August I'll start checking the mouth of the Sakonnet and the rips off Napatree for the first signs. For now, if I've only got one trip this week, I'm fishing the last two hours of dark at Sakonnet Point on the outgoing, bucktail and rind, and I'm covering the Jamestown flats midday on the moving water for fluke. Both are producing consistent enough numbers to be worth the drive, as long as you respect the tide and don't waste time fishing it slack.
